items.title: An N for a new sequence
items.question: What is the smallest $N$ that works for $\varepsilon = 0.01$?

byKey.edge: At $n = 149$ the gap is $\tfrac{3}{299} \approx 0.01003$, just above 0.01.
byKey.no-half: You solved $n > 300$. The condition is $2n + 1 > 300$, so $n > 149.5$.

items.title: A quotient proof with a hole
items.prose: This attempted proof that $\tfrac{1}{b_n} \to \tfrac1b$ assumes $b_n \to b$, $b \ne 0$ and every $b_n \ne 0$. One line is false.
items.question: Tap the false line.

feedback.correct: Right. Line 4 needs $|b_n| \ge |b|$, which can fail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each line with $b = 1$ and $b_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1}$.

byKey.r1: Line 2 is a fair choice: $\varepsilon |b|^2 > 0$, so such an $N$ exists.
byKey.r2: Line 3 is algebra: put both fractions over $b_nb$.
byKey.r4: Line 5 follows from lines 2 and 4. The false claim is earlier.

explain.text: With $b = 1$ and $b_n = 1 - \tfrac{1}{n+1}$, line 3 gives $\tfrac1n$ but line 4 claims at most $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$. The quotient proof first takes $N$ with $|b_n| > \tfrac{|b|}{2}$. That gives the bound $\tfrac{2|b_n - b|}{|b|^2}$ instead.

items.title: A recursion, honestly
items.prose: Let $a_1 = 2$ and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{6 + a_n}$: $2, 2.8284, 2.9713, 2.9952, \dots$ The limit equation $L = \sqrt{6 + L}$ has the squared form $L^2 - L - 6 = 0$, with roots 3 and $-2$.
items.question: Which argument proves $a_n \to 3$?

options.text: Induction gives $a_n < a_{n+1} < 3$. Monotone convergence gives a limit $L \ge 2$; then $L = \sqrt{6 + L}$ forces $L = 3$.

options.why: You solved for $L$ without showing a limit exists. The same move gives $L = 0$ for $a_{n+1} = 2a_n$, which diverges.

options.text: The terms 2.9952 and 2.9992 are close to 3.
options.why: You read off computed terms. A few terms near 3 prove nothing about the tail.

options.text: The terms are bounded by 3, so they converge to 3.
options.why: You used boundedness alone. Bounded sequences such as $(-1)^n$ can diverge; monotone is needed too.

feedback.correct: Right. Bounded and monotone first, then the fixed point.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A limit equation is valid only after convergence is proved.

explain.text: If $a_n < a_{n+1} < 3$, then $6 + a_n < 6 + a_{n+1} < 9$, and roots give $a_{n+1} < a_{n+2} < 3$. Monotone convergence gives $L$, and every $a_n \ge 2$ rules out $-2$. So $a_n \to 3$.

options.why: You took every even index. Those terms are $-1, 1, -1, 1$, which do not converge.
You took the odd indices. Those terms are all 0, so they converge to 0.
You took indices 2, 6, 10. Those terms are all $-1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the terms each subsequence picks.

explain.text: $a_{4k} = \cos(2k\pi) = 1$, a constant subsequence. The odd terms tend to 0 and $a_{4k-2} = -1$. Three different subsequential limits: the sequence diverges.

items.title: Cauchy or not
items.prose: Four sequences, each with steps that tend to 0 or stay small.
items.question: Which one is Cauchy?

options.why: You judged by the steps. $H_{2n} - H_n \ge \tfrac12$ for every $n$, so it is not Cauchy.
You judged by the steps. $\sqrt{4n} - \sqrt n = \sqrt n \ge 1$, so it is not Cauchy.
You judged by the steps. $\ln(2n) - \ln n = \ln 2$ for every $n$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare terms far apart, not only neighbours.

explain.text: For $m > n$, $S_m - S_n = \tfrac{1}{2^{n+1}} + \cdots + \tfrac{1}{2^m} < \tfrac{1}{2^n}$. That falls below any $\varepsilon$, so $(S_n)$ is Cauchy. Each of the other three has pairs past any $N$ at least a fixed distance apart.

items.title: A threshold in epsilon
items.question: $|a_n - 1| < \varepsilon$ exactly when $n$ is greater than what?

byKey.plus: You added 1. To get $n$ alone from $n + 1$, subtract 1.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{n+1} < \varepsilon \iff n + 1 > \tfrac1\varepsilon \iff n > \tfrac1\varepsilon - 1$. At $\varepsilon = 0.1$ that is $n > 9$, so $N = 10$. Check: $\tfrac{1}{11} \approx 0.091$.

items.title: Three sequences, one N
items.prose: Let $a_n = 1 + \tfrac1n$, $b_n = 2 - \tfrac2n$ and $c_n = 3 + \tfrac3n$, with $\varepsilon = 0.3$. A sum law for three sequences asks each gap to be below $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} = 0.1$.
items.question: What $N$ does that proof choose?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each first index for 0.1, then take the largest.

byKey.min: You took the smallest index. Between 11 and 31 the $c_n$ gap is still 0.1 or more.
byKey.direct: You found the sum's own first index: $|a_n + b_n + c_n - 6| = \tfrac2n < 0.3$ from 7. The proof's recipe gives 31.
byKey.half: You split $\varepsilon$ in two. Three gaps need $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$ each, so that their sum stays below $\varepsilon$.

explain.text: $\tfrac1n$, $\tfrac2n$ and $\tfrac3n$ drop below 0.1 from 11, 21 and 31, so the proof takes 31. Three gaps each below $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{3}$ add to less than $\varepsilon$. Directly, $\tfrac2n < 0.3$ from $n = 7$, so 31 is valid but not sharp.

items.title: A limit you can solve for
items.prose: Let $a_1 = 1$ and $a_{n+1} = \tfrac{a_n + 8}{3}$: $1, 3, \tfrac{11}{3}, \tfrac{35}{9}, \dots$ Induction shows it rises and stays below 4.
items.question: What is its limit?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $L = \tfrac{L + 8}{3}$, valid now that a limit exists.

byKey.eight-thirds: You dropped the $L$ on the right. The equation is $3L = L + 8$.
byKey.eight: You took the constant 8. The equation $3L = L + 8$ gives $L = 4$.

explain.text: Rising and bounded by 4, so a limit exists. Then $3L = L + 8$ gives $L = 4$. The gap to 4 shrinks by a factor of 3 each step: 3, 1, $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac19$.

items.title: One strand decides
items.prose: $(a_n)$ is Cauchy, and its subsequence $(a_{2k})$ tends to 5.
items.question: What can we conclude?

options.text: $a_n \to 5$: the whole sequence follows its subsequence.

options.why: You ignored the Cauchy condition. Each odd term past $N$ is within $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ of an even term past $N$.
You stopped too early. Bounded is the first step; the Cauchy condition then forces the limit 5.

options.text: The odd terms may tend to another limit.
options.why: You allowed two limits. A Cauchy sequence converges, and its subsequences share its limit.

feedback.correct: Right. Cauchy plus one convergent subsequence gives convergence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the last step of the Cauchy-implies-convergent proof.

explain.text: Pick $N$ for $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and an even index $2k \ge N$ with $|a_{2k} - 5| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$. For $n \ge N$, $|a_n - 5| \le |a_n - a_{2k}| + |a_{2k} - 5| < \varepsilon$. So $a_n \to 5$.
